newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korean subway drivers back down, unions fight on.
newsitem.headline: Korean subway drivers back down, unions fight on.

text.p: Striking South Korean subway drivers and nurses began drifting back to work on Monday, but labour union leaders said it was only a temporary retreat and vowed to escalate industrial action in the new year.
Shipyards and car plants remained idle, and the central bank figures showed strikes that have swept the country since Thursday were hitting exports.
"We will take our strikes to a higher level and prolong them starting in the new year," said Kwon Young-kil, head of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.

The much larger Federation of Korean Trade Unions, which called its 1.2 million members out on strike until the end of the year, said it would announce details on Tuesday on "an escalated second stage which would include the public sector".

Striking subway drivers in Seoul and South Korea's second-biggest city, Pusan, returned to their posts on Monday after a short strike failed to disrupt services. Non-union workers had kept trains moving.
Subway unions are discussing a renewed strike in January, and the Seoul Metropolitan Rapid Transit, which runs three new lines in Seoul, has already declared a 48-hour strike starting on Saturday.
Hospital unions decided to suspend their action on Tuesday, although some nurses and orderlies began returning to their wards on Sunday and more joined them on Monday.
Transport and medical unions said they were suspending industrial action to spare the public from chaos over the New Year holiday period.

Students, who have kept a low profile since a major crackdown by the government in August, took to the streets to support workers and to protest against the law which was rammed thorough a dawn sitting of parliament on Thursday when opposition legislators were still asleep.
The law allows companies to lay off workers, replace strikers, and hire temporary staff.

Chanting anti-government slogans, 1,000 students rallied in Myung-dong, Seoul's commercial centre, witnesses said. They sat in a pedestian zone and faced a wall of riot police in full gear armed with teargas rifles.

Earlier, riot police grabbed shopkeepers whom they mistook for students, prompting a protest from fellow merchants, according to witnesses. Some stores closed in anticipation of clashes, but the rally ended peacefully.
In a silent march on a busy downtown street, 50 university professors with sashes draped across their chests staged a protest against the labour law and a law to strengthen Korea's spy agency.
Despite the waves of strikes and daily worker protests sparked by the passage, the cabinet on Monday approved the labour law, setting it in stone.
Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung, in a televised speech on Monday, warned workers that "legal countermeasures" would be taken to stop strikes.
Lee defended the law saying it was the only way to boost a fragile economy.
"We chose the law to prevent our offspring from falling behind developing countries," Lee said. "We could not watch companies go bankrupt and corporations move offshore, causing major job losses."
Union members at Korea Telecom, the state telecommunications giant, were voting on whether to strike in the New Year, and a decision was expected by Tuesday afternoon, union officials said.
Tellers and clerks at local banks voted to strike for one day on Saturday.
The central bank said strikes would help swell South Korea's current account deficit this year to more than $22 billion from its earlier forecast of about $21.5 billion.

"Traditionally, we've seen strong exports at the year end. But that's unlikely to be the case this year with labour strikes hindering exports during the last week of this month," said bank official Paeng Dong-joon. "At this point, the current account deficit is seen well above $22 billion for the year."
